doc.title: Mike Wofford interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

title: Current work and his experimental group Live Music
summary: He works mostly in San Diego, recently recorded with Ray Brown and Ralph Moore, and leads Live Music, an exploratory group with violin, cello and bass clarinet.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: That’s great. What’s in the close future for you? More of the same?

Well I still travel some. I stay primarily in San Diego. I do some work in L.A. I just was up there earlier this week, I worked with Ray Brown on some recordings up there, with a wonderful — the first time I’d worked with him, I’d admired him on recordings but first time I’d met him or worked with him, Ralph Moore, a wonderful tenor and soprano player. Marvelous. He is now in L.A. I didn’t realize that. I thought he was still in New York but you know so many guys have moved out here, and I had a drummer named Greg Hutchinson, whose a marvelous young drummer. Ralph’s out here to do The Tonight Show. He’s part of The Tonight Show band, Jay Leno’s show. So that’s what he’s doing out here. So anyway I do get up there to do some things, but I’ve become more interested in kind of experimental music and it’s still jazz oriented but I’ve moved away from mainstream jazz as such, as far as my own projects. I still do a certain amount of that when I’m called to do so you know. But I have a group here in San Diego called Live Music which is an interesting combination of instrumentation.

It’s primarily still acoustic, but the violinist, who is also a guitarist, Art Johnson, who was in Los Angeles for years, uses electric violin at times. But it’s primarily an acoustic group, acoustic bass and drums, but cello and bass clarinet and various interesting combinations of instruments, and we’re doing a lot more exploratory kind of improvisational music. It’s really probably closer to the classical world than jazz as such, although everyone is from the jazz world, all the players are. So I’m more and more, as far as my own personal projects, I’m more interested in where do we go from here.
Do you recall a record by Roger Kellaway, the “Cello Quartet?”
That was some nice stuff there.
